method: Converts RAID geometry into the ext4 stride and stripe-width values. The chunk size in KiB is multiplied by 1024 to bytes, and the stride is that figure divided by the filesystem block size, which must leave no remainder: chunk sizes are whole KiB values from 4 to 4096 and multiples of 4, so the 1, 2 and 4 KiB block sizes always divide exactly and every result is a whole number of blocks. The data-disk count follows the RAID level: all members for RAID 0, one for a single disk or a mirror, members minus one for RAID 5, members minus two for RAID 6, and half the members for RAID 10, which is the near-2 layout mdadm creates by default and therefore requires an even member count. The stripe width is the stride multiplied by the data disks, and one full stripe is the chunk multiplied by the data disks. Arrays are limited to 1 to 64 members with the minimum member count of each level enforced: 2 for RAID 0, RAID 1 and RAID 10, 3 for RAID 5 and 4 for RAID 6. The commands shown are mkfs.ext4 with -b and -E stride,stripe-width, and the equivalent mkfs.xfs -d su,sw with the parity disks excluded from sw; when the array has no striping the stride options are omitted and said to be unnecessary. A stride below four blocks is reported as too narrow to matter. Anything outside those bounds, a non-numeric or out-of-range disk count, a chunk that is not a multiple of 4 KiB, an unsupported block size, or a RAID level the member count cannot satisfy is refused with the field named rather than coerced. Not modelled: partition and 1 MiB alignment, 4Kn and 512e sector sizes, SSD erase blocks and zoned storage, thin provisioning and snapshots, far or offset RAID 10 layouts, XFS stripe width handling on parity arrays beyond excluding parity from sw, and measured throughput. Pure local arithmetic: no storage, uploads or network access.
